query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Controlled thermal annealing of the as‐cast, non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEA promotes the diffusion‐driven segregation of Mg into stable intermetallic precipitates that preferentially form at grain boundaries. These Mg-rich precipitates create local galvanic cells, which accelerate localized corrosion, while at the same time they act as nucleation sites for a uniform, protective oxide scale at high temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, induction-melted MgAlCuZnGd high-entropy alloy with a non-equilibrium microstructure comprising a mixture of solid solution regions and metastable intermetallic compounds.
generation.intervention: Subject the as-cast alloy to a controlled isothermal annealing treatment (at a specified T_anneal for a defined t_anneal) designed to drive the transformation of the metastable state into an equilibrium state with well-developed Mg-rich intermetallic phases.
generation.conditions: Annealing is performed under an inert atmosphere at a controlled temperature (T_anneal) and time (t_anneal) optimized for phase segregation; subsequent corrosion tests are conducted in a standard corrosive medium, and high-temperature oxidation tests are performed under a controlled oxidizing environment at the target evaluation temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and coarsening of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates, particularly at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: During annealing, Mg atoms diffuse and segregate to form discrete intermetallic precipitates. The interfaces between these precipitates and the surrounding matrix create micro-galvanic cells that accelerate localized corrosion. Simultaneously, these precipitates act as nucleation sites during high-temperature exposure, leading to the development of a coherent, protective oxide scale which improves oxidation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, the annealed alloy will show increased susceptibility to localized corrosion (i.e., a deterioration in corrosion resistance) while displaying an improved high-temperature oxidation behavior as evidenced by a more protective and uniform oxide scale.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy (density < 6 g/cm3) before any post-treatment.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies within the design constraint of alloys with a density below 6 g/cm3, where processing conditions maintain partial metastability; evaluation is restricted to standardized corrosion and high-temperature oxidation testing conditions as specified by the testing protocols.
generation.uncertainty: The exact annealing temperature, time, and quantitative changes in corrosion rate and oxide scale properties are not fully defined and would require optimization through further experimental work.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of MgAlCuZnGd alloy samples: one set in the as-cast state (baseline) and the other set subjected to the specified isothermal annealing treatment. Expose both sets to identical standardized corrosion testing (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization) and high-temperature oxidation testing protocols. Use microstructural and compositional analyses (e.g., SEM, TEM, XRD) to characterize precipitate formation and oxide scale characteristics.
measurements: Electrochemical measurements (e.g., corrosion current density, passivation behavior)
Oxide scale thickness, uniformity, and composition (via SEM/EDS and XRD)
Microstructural analysis for precipitate size/distribution (via TEM/SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed alloy does not exhibit both a statistically significant increase in micro-galvanic corrosion indicators (e.g., higher localized corrosion rates) and improved high-temperature oxidation characteristics (e.g., formation of a more uniform and protective oxide scale) relative to the as-cast baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.
